content:
This PR develops the notion of euclidean rings in the sense of Samuel (1970), “About Euclidean Rings”, Journal of Algebra 19, p. 282-301.

It is added for discussion mainly. The interest of the definition is that it is more general than the classical one, and it gives rise to a predicate for a ring to be euclidean (in a more general sense) which, except for computational purposes, is as good as the definition in mathlib.

The point is that there is a minimal stathm, which corresponds to a canonical increasing Set-filtration of the ring indexed by Ordinal. The ring is euclidean (in the generalized sense) if and only if the filtration is exhaustive.

Antoine Chambert-Loir said:

The interest of the definition is that it is more general than the classical one

I am a bit puzzled by the "more general" part here; it seems to me that our docs#EuclideanDomain already covers this generality, because we allow for an arbitrary well-founded relation instead of a nat-valued function. Thus I would expect your IsOrdinalEuclidean to be equivalent to the existence of a docs#EuclideanDomain structure on the ring, is that not the case?

Of course, even if it does not increase generality, your PR is still useful because we'd rather assume a Prop-valued class rather than data in theorems that don't need the extra data !
Also, are there any useful results that hold under IsNatEuclidean but not IsOrdinalEuclidean ?

Apparently not. Except that, according to Samuel, Z×Z\mathbf Z\times\mathbf ZZ×Z is Ord-euclidean but not Nat-euclidean! Samuel writes he doesn't know whether the notions differ for general domains (but he proves that they coincide for domains with finite residue fields, eg, finitely generated Z\mathbf ZZ-algebras which are domain: in this case, the smallest algorithm is Nat-valued).

Regarding the generality, the filtration gives the smallest possible stathm (gauge, norm, whatever) on a euclidean ring, hence the equivalence that you say is (likely) true, up to the Prop/data distinction, and up to the admission of arbitrary semirings. (I say “likely”, because the well founded relation on a euclidean domain is possibly not totally ordered. Update: that works, and is already explained in Samuel's paper.)

But, as you said, the goal was just to show that mathematically, euclidean rings can be defined by a property rather than data. (Computationally, it is another matter, especially to be able to compute the division with remainder.)

Actually there is a difference, since Mathlib's docs#EuclideanDomain does imply docs#IsDomain. IIUC this is because of axiom docs#EuclideanDomain.mul_left_not_lt ? French Wikipedia claims that this condition can always be forced in a domain, but probably not in general ?

Samuel explains that a principal ideal ring is a finite product of principal ideal domains and of principal ideal local rings whose maximal ideal is nilpotent. And he adds that this should explain the lack of interest in general principal ideal rings.

If I'm not mistaken, Samuel's proposition 4 shows that a given stathm ϕ\phiϕ can be modified so as to satisfy this condition (trivially, setting ϕ1(a)\phi_1(a)ϕ1​(a) to be the minimal value of ϕ(x)\phi(x)ϕ(x) on nonzero multiples of aaa), leading to a smaller stathm. So the minimal one should satisfy this as well.
